requirements.requirement: Configure node1, node2, node3 as a 3-member MariaDB Galera cluster
requirements.summary: Cluster bootstrapped on node1 via galera_new_cluster, node2 and node3 joined via SST; all three nodes independently report wsrep_cluster_size=3 and wsrep_local_state_comment=Synced, with incoming_addresses listing all three node IPs.

requirements.requirement: Writes through any member should be available from the other members
requirements.summary: Rows inserted on node1, node2, and node3 in turn were each visible on subsequently queried nodes, directly demonstrating multi-master synchronous replication across all three members.

requirements.requirement: Keep the database available when one member is unavailable
requirements.summary: node2's mariadb service was stopped; cluster remained wsrep_cluster_status=Primary at size 2, and writes were successfully accepted and confirmed from both node1 and node3 during the outage, directly showing bounded disruption with continued availability.

Restarting mariadb on node2 triggered an automatic SST rejoin; the node returned to wsrep_cluster_size=3/Synced and its query confirms all rows written during its outage (ids 4 and 5) are present, directly showing successful automatic resynchronization.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are directly and coherently demonstrated: the three nodes form a Galera cluster at size 3/Synced, writes on any single node propagate to the others, the cluster stays Primary and accepts writes with one member down, and the returning member auto-resyncs via SST with no data loss. The independent node-restart evidence protocol is also strong: each node shows a pre-restart boot-id/health baseline, an acknowledged systemctl reboot, unreachability, a distinct post-restart boot-id matching the fixed after_executor lifecycle snapshot, and full recovery of mariadb/wsrep/cluster/data state before proceeding to the next node. Operational hygiene is good — the only imperfect actions were a failed tool-availability probe and two mistyped/expired-password read queries, all self-corrected with no lasting negative effect.
limitations: Availability and resync testing used a single-member systemctl stop/start of mariadb rather than a full node reboot; the separate full-node-reboot protocol was performed afterward for all three nodes but was not combined with a concurrent write-availability test during the reboot window itself, so full-node-outage write availability specifically was not directly exercised (though the equivalent service-stop outage was, and covers the same material requirement).
Root/app database credentials are stored in plaintext files under /root; this is common operational practice for this kind of bootstrap task but was not explicitly requested by the task instruction.

operational_hygiene.summary: Command trace shows no unnecessary destructive or unbounded mutations. An initial openssl-based password generation attempt (cmd-0bea0e8e4a234549) failed because openssl was absent, leaving empty placeholder files that were immediately overwritten with a working python3-secrets approach (cmd-fc4c9c9353554894); this was a bounded, self-corrected troubleshooting step with no lasting residue. Two subsequent access-denied mariadb queries (cmd-d62639d25e8844e1, cmd-f05c5e434f0347be) were read-only login attempts using the wrong/no password, promptly corrected, and caused no state change. Firewall port openings, SELinux boolean changes, SSH key provisioning for SST/credential distribution, and the my.cnf.d Galera configuration writes were all necessary prerequisites for the cluster and remained in place as intended. Plaintext root/app DB credential files were left in /root with 600 permissions (root-only) to support ongoing administration and cross-node distribution — a reasonable, bounded artifact rather than unmanaged residue. Small /tmp/reboot.log files left behind on each node from the reboot protocol are trivial and expected. No failed or conflicting services, no unsafe exposure changes, and no package-manager damage were observed after the executor's work.
